name: Buraco
description: Buraco is a popular Rummy-type card game family originating in South America, played with partnerships and featuring unique mechanics like the morto (extra hand). The main variants are Brazilian Buraco (Canastra/Biriba), Italian Burraco, and Argentinean Burako (tile version). Games are played with double decks and involve melding sequences to create canastas.

content.text: Buraco is a popular Rummy-type card game family originating in South America, played with partnerships and featuring unique mechanics like the morto (extra hand). The main variants are Brazilian Buraco (Canastra/Biriba), Italian Burraco, and Argentinean Burako (tile version). Games are played with double decks and involve melding sequences to create canastas.

Buraco originated in South America, probably in the 1940s, likely in Brazil or Argentina. The game evolved from Canasta and shares similarities with Samba. The name comes from Portuguese/Spanish and refers to the 'hole' or extra hand mechanic.
104-108 cards: two standard 52-card decks plus 0-4 jokers depending on variant
Double deck with jokers, score sheet, table space for melds
Two 11-card mortos (extra hands) set aside. Each player receives 11 cards. Remaining cards form draw pile. Brazilian: 108 cards with 4 jokers; Italian: 104 cards no jokers; twos often wild.

items.text: Buraco Fechado (Closed Buraco): Variation where the discard pile is closed (only the top card is visible), sets of equal rank are allowed as melds, and a canastra of twos can score a higher bonus; going out only requires at least one canastra, not necessarily clean.
Alternative Target Scores: Some groups play to a target of 2000 or 3500 points instead of the standard 3000, ending the match when a team reaches or passes the chosen total.
Rounded Scoring to Tens: In some tables all scores are rounded up to the nearest multiple of ten, for example 485 is recorded as 490 on the running score sheet.
No Vulnerability Requirement: Some play without the vulnerability rule, so there is no minimum opening meld value even after a team has reached half of the target score.
High-Value Jokers: A common scoring variation treats each joker as worth 50 points instead of the standard 20, increasing the impact of wild cards in melds and in hand.
No Jokers, Only Twos Wild: Some play with no jokers in the deck so that only the twos act as wild cards, giving a 106-card pack while keeping the same meld structure.

Alternative Canastra Bonuses: Some groups score 150 points for a dirty canastra and 300 for a clean one, count a clean set of all eight cards of a rank as a canastra real worth 1000 points, or award extra bonuses for special cutting situations.
